In Great Expectations, Charles Dickens gives Pip exactly what he wants, money, education, and a way out of the marsh village and Joe's forge, and then shows that every step up costs him the one place where he was loved without conditions. Pip's ambition isn't wicked on its own, since it starts with a boy being made to feel small. But Dickens builds the novel so that Pip's rise and his exile are one movement. In the end the book suggests that being a "gentleman" in Victorian England meant learning to be ashamed of where you came from, and that real worth is found in the loyalty Pip spent most of the novel running away from.

The ambition is born at Satis House, and the scene is important because it shows ambition and shame arriving together. Before he meets Estella, Pip is not exactly happy with Mrs. Joe, but he doesn't think of the forge as low. Then Estella mocks his rough hands and his boots and the common way he talks about cards, and Pip goes home looking at Joe through her eyes. Dickens makes the desire to rise and the contempt for home happen at the same moment. Pip doesn't want to be a gentleman for its own sake. He wants it so he will never be looked at like that again, which means his ambition is already, from the start, a rejection of the people who raised him.

When Jaggers announces Pip's "great expectations," the distance becomes physical as well as emotional. The most painful example is Joe's visit to London. Joe, who is comfortable and dignified at the forge, becomes clumsy in Pip's rooms. He keeps fumbling with his hat and calls Pip "sir," and Pip is relieved when he leaves. What makes this scene so effective is the narration. The older Pip telling the story clearly sees his younger self's snobbery and is embarrassed by it, so the reader gets two views together: young Pip's discomfort with Joe, and the older narrator's judgment of that discomfort. The first-person retrospective point of view turns the scene into a confession, and that keeps the novel from simply celebrating Pip's success.

Dickens's biggest complication comes with Magwitch. Pip has assumed Miss Havisham is his benefactor, which fits his dream of rising into a refined world, maybe even being meant for Estella. Instead the money comes from the convict he helped on the marshes as a child. This twist undercuts the whole idea of gentility. The "gentleman" was made by a criminal, out of a criminal's gratitude, so the class line Pip worked so hard to cross turns out to be partly an illusion. You could read the novel as just a warning against ambition, but Magwitch makes it harder than that. Pip's disgust with Magwitch is the same snobbery he showed toward Joe, and he only grows when he learns to care for Magwitch anyway. It isn't wanting more that Dickens condemns. It's a system that teaches Pip that wanting more means despising those below him.

The ending doesn't completely heal the split, and this makes the argument more honest. Joe nurses Pip through his illness and quietly pays off his debts, which shows that the belonging Pip left behind was still there for him. But Pip can't just go back. Joe marries Biddy, and Pip leaves to work abroad with Herbert. The forge is still home, but it is no longer Pip's home, because his ambition changed him too much to fit back in. Even the uncertain final meeting with Estella feels less like a happy reward than a scene between two people who have been damaged by the same false expectations. Dickens lets Pip become a better man, but not a man who belongs anywhere, and that is the real price of his rise.

input.essay:
When Pip finds out he has "great expectations," the news seems like a way out of the marshes, the forge, and a life he has already learned to be ashamed of. Charles Dickens doesn't treat Pip's ambition as simply a mistake, though. In Great Expectations the drive to become a gentleman really does pull Pip out of a cramped, sometimes cruel home, but it also teaches him to see the people who loved him through the eyes of the people who looked down on him. The novel suggests that ambition built on shame cuts a person off from belonging, and that the only success worth having is the one Pip finds at the end, when he is poor and humbled and able to go back home.

Pip's ambition starts as a wound, not a dream. At Satis House, Estella mocks his coarse hands and thick boots, and Miss Havisham watches it happen. Before this visit Pip had no reason to think the forge was low. Afterward he can't stop seeing it as low. Dickens makes the point that ambition can be planted from outside: Pip's longing to rise comes from humiliation by a class that has no real affection for him. That is why it divides him from Joe so quickly. Once he wants Estella's approval, he has to hold Joe in contempt, even though Joe is the one adult who protected him from Mrs. Joe's rages.

The clearest picture of this split is Joe's visit to London. Joe, uncomfortable in his good clothes, keeps calling Pip "sir," and his hat keeps sliding off the mantel while Pip winces and wishes he would leave. The scene is funny, but it hurts, because the comedy is told from inside Pip's embarrassment. The older Pip narrating the story knows how badly he acted, and that double vision matters. We see the young man's snobbery and the grown man's regret together, so the scene shows both what ambition has gotten Pip, polish and a place in London, and what it has cost him, the ease of simply being loved. Joe gets this better than Pip does. He leaves saying, in effect, that they belong in different places now, and it sounds less like an insult than like grief.

Someone could argue that Pip owed nothing to the marsh community, which wasn't much of a community. Mrs. Joe raises him "by hand" and treats him like a burden, Pumblechook bullies him, and Orlick is dangerous. That objection has some force, and Dickens doesn't make the village into paradise. But Joe and Biddy are a different kind of belonging, one based on loyalty instead of status, and the plot tests which kind is real. The twist that Magwitch, not Miss Havisham, is Pip's benefactor wrecks the fantasy that Pip's rise was refined or deserved. His gentility was paid for by a transported convict, the same man he fed on the marshes as a frightened child. In this way the structure of the novel drags Pip's ambition back to the place it was trying to escape. The marshes were never really behind him.

This is why the ending works as a return and not just as a punishment. Pip learns to love Magwitch and stays loyal to him as he dies, which is the first time he chooses a bond over appearances. Then Pip falls ill, and it is Joe who nurses him and quietly pays his debts. Pip goes back intending to propose to Biddy and finds she has married Joe, so he can't simply step back into the old life either. He works abroad with Herbert and earns a modest living by honest labor. Dickens doesn't give him the triumph he wanted, or a full homecoming. What Pip gets is the self-knowledge that lets him tell the story the way he does: an ambition that once separated him from belonging becomes, in hindsight, the way he learns what belonging was worth.

In The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald, Jay Gatsby is a very ambitious character who wants to be rich and successful. His ambition takes him away from his family and where he came from, and this shows that ambition can be both good and bad.

Gatsby was born James Gatz in North Dakota to poor farmers. He changes his name and becomes Jay Gatsby, which shows he wants to leave his past behind. He meets Dan Cody and then later gets rich, probably from bootlegging with Meyer Wolfsheim. He buys a huge mansion in West Egg across the water from Daisy. He has big parties every weekend where lots of people come, but he does not really know them. This shows that he is successful but he has no real friends or belonging.

Daisy is the main reason for his ambition. He wants to get her back so he gets rich. But Daisy is married to Tom Buchanan, who is old money. Gatsby tries to show her his shirts and his house but it does not work out. At the end Gatsby dies in his pool and almost nobody comes to his funeral. Nick says some things about him. His father Henry Gatz comes to the funeral and is proud of him. This shows that Gatsby was alone even though he had worked so hard.

The green light is also a symbol of Gatsby's dream. He is always reaching for it but he can never get it. In conclusion, Gatsby's ambition made him successful but it also made him lonely, and the book shows that ambition can cost you belonging.

input.essay:
In The Great Gatsby, F. Scott Fitzgerald shows that Jay Gatsby's ambition to become somebody carries him away from the people and place that made him, and that this success leaves him with nothing to belong to. Gatsby's rise is therefore less a triumph than a kind of exile, and the novel uses it to question whether the American dream can ever really be reached.

Gatsby begins as James Gatz, the son of poor farming people in North Dakota, and he decides at a young age to invent a new self. When he meets Dan Cody he leaves his family behind and takes a new name, so his ambition requires cutting off where he came from. This shows that for Gatsby success means escaping his origins rather than building on them. Later, he tells Nick a story about being from a wealthy family in the Midwest, which is a lie meant to hide his real background. The fact that he has to lie about his past shows that the belonging he lost was never replaced by anything real.

Gatsby's house in West Egg is another example. He becomes extremely rich and throws huge parties, but the guests mostly do not know him and come only for the free drinks and entertainment. Nick notices that people gossip about Gatsby without caring about him. The crowds are large, but Gatsby stands apart and watches, so Fitzgerald is showing that his money has bought attention but not community. Even more, West Egg is separated from East Egg, where Daisy lives, by the bay, and this geography shows how Gatsby can see what he wants but cannot truly join it. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this, because it is always visible but out of reach. Gatsby's ambition is really aimed at Daisy and the old-money world she represents, and that world never accepts him, as shown when Tom exposes him in the hotel scene.

The ending of the novel makes the tension clearest. After Gatsby is killed, almost nobody comes to his funeral, and the people from his parties do not appear. The only family member who comes is his father, who is proud of his son's success, which is a sad contrast with how Gatsby had hidden his family. This moment suggests that the belonging Gatsby gave up was the only kind that was left to him at the end. Nick, who narrates, is from the Midwest too, and he decides to go back, which implies that the novel sees some value in the place Gatsby ran from.

Overall, Fitzgerald presents Gatsby's ambition as both admirable and tragic. His dream is a hopeful one, but it costs him his roots and leaves him alone, which makes the novel a warning about success that is cut off from belonging.

input.essay:
In The Great Gatsby, Jay Gatsby's ambition carries him far from the poor family and the North Dakota farm life he was born into, but Fitzgerald shows that the success he reaches for never gives him a place to belong. The novel suggests that the American dream of self-invention turns into a kind of exile, because Gatsby builds a new self by cutting off the old one and then finds that the world he wants to enter will not accept him.

Gatsby's break with his origins is clear in the way he changes his name from James Gatz and invents a past. Nick learns that Gatsby sprang from "his Platonic conception of himself," and that he took up with Dan Cody, a rich man who gave him his first taste of wealth. This shows that Gatsby's ambition requires him to leave behind his family and community completely. He does not just move away, he erases where he came from. The invented story about being the son of wealthy people in the Midwest shows that he thinks belonging has to be bought with a false identity. Fitzgerald uses this to suggest that ambition in the novel is not about becoming better, but about becoming someone else.

The house and the parties show the cost of this. Gatsby buys a mansion in West Egg across the water from Daisy, and he throws huge parties where hundreds of strangers come and drink. But the guests do not really know him, and they gossip about him instead. The setting of West Egg versus East Egg also matters, because it shows that Gatsby has money but is still on the wrong side of a social divide. Tom and Daisy belong to old money, so Gatsby can be at the edge of their world but never inside it. The green light at the end of Daisy's dock is a symbol of this, since it is always visible but out of reach. Gatsby's dream pulls him forward while keeping him separate from what he wants.

The ending makes this point most strongly. When Gatsby is killed, almost nobody comes to his funeral, even though so many people came to his parties. Only Nick, a few servants, and his father, Henry Gatz, who comes from the Midwest, are there. The father's appearance is important because it brings back the family Gatsby had tried to leave, and it is the only real belonging he gets, but it comes too late. Nick says at the end that we are "borne back ceaselessly into the past," which suggests that the past Gatsby ran from is what he could not escape.

In the end Fitzgerald presents Gatsby's ambition as both admirable and tragic. His determination is impressive, but it leaves him alone. The novel's meaning is that success which depends on abandoning where you came from cannot give you a home.
